toc.title: What changes when safety is there too

blocks.p: A listener sent me this question:

q: I'm not a therapist. I just really love learning about psychology and trauma. I wanted to ask you a question I've meant to ask a therapist for a while now. If you can't answer, I completely understand.

In the book The Bell Jar, two characters are talking, and one asks the main character if she would rather live in the city or the country, and she says she can't decide, and she'd probably want to live in between to have equal access to both. Her friend responds by laughing and says that she has the perfect setup for a neurotic because she wants two mutually exclusive things at the same time.

This has been burned into my memory, and I constantly think about it when I find myself wanting two mutually exclusive things at once or just having a hard time making decisions. The book is from a different era, and people were less informed, and I'm not even sure what being labeled as a neurotic means, but I was wondering if you could explain this through a polyvagal lens.

blocks.p: I don't know exactly what a neurotic is either. I have an image of it in my mind, but I don't know how helpful that is. So I'll leave that word aside and answer the rest.
First off, I don't really think things are mutually exclusive. I think it's totally possible, and maybe even a good idea, to hold a couple of different feelings in your body at once.

Let's start there. You may have some stuck defensive energy. That's what trauma would be: being stuck in an autonomic nervous system state of defense, so flight, fight, shutdown, or the mixed state of freeze. Having a couple of different feelings at once isn't a bad thing. It's completely possible, and probably a very good idea when it comes to balancing your feelings out.

In session, a common thing I do is help people feel that stuck defensive stuff, flight, fight, shutdown, or freeze, whatever it is, enough that it's there but not overwhelming. We notice it. We don't try to make it go away. We don't minimize it. We don't excuse it. We actually invite it to be with us: "Hey, what's up? I see you. I see you feeling. Come on, hang out with me while I do my therapy session with Justin." So it's okay to have that feeling, and also have another feeling at the same time.

That other feeling is safety. Before going into the difficult stuff, I help people identify what safety feels like. You would think defensiveness and safety are mutually exclusive, but they're not. These are both feelings we have to be able to have and to balance, and I would say have at the same time, especially when we're working on trauma. We have to be able to feel safety as well: to activate those ventral vagal pathways, to be more grounded in the present moment, to feel connected with me as a therapist, or whoever's in your life, or with yourself. So we have to be able to feel grounded and connected, and also feel the stuck defensive energy.

blocks.h: What changes when safety is there too

blocks.p: When you do that, the defense becomes something different. It's kind of a blend.

Without safety, the stuck freeze state can feel like out-of-control panic, or even rage, as it comes up and hopefully comes out. Once safety is active along with it, it won't be this out-of-control, rageful, panicky thing. We'll be able to notice those feelings, stay with them, breathe through them, talk about them, feel them, and then watch as they shift, or consciously notice as they shift, to something else. It just won't be that anymore.

If you don't have the safety state active when you go to the more defensive stuff, then it is felt as panic or rage or whatever it is. And then it just gets fed back into the system, because it doesn't actually discharge. Nothing changes. There's no shift. Maybe we power through talking about something difficult, but then it's the same thing all over again. It doesn't actually help. It's basically re-traumatizing.
So these are two different feelings you'd think are mutually exclusive, but they're really necessary at the same time.

Wanting things that are external to us is a different matter. Say you can't decide between living in one place or another, or between a chocolate muffin and a blueberry muffin. It's okay to want two things at once. So what?

That's a decision. What do you think is best? You may rationally think they're both fantastic. You may rationally say, "Living here or living here would both do something for me," and that's true. There's nothing wrong with that.

I could be completely missing the point of the story, but to me, living in the middle is saying, "I want both of these things, and now I have equal access to both of them." That's like dividing a muffin in half: now I can have both. Awesome. To me, that's problem solving. I don't see that as neurotic. If anything, I think it's less healthy to demand that somebody know exactly what they want and stick to it, especially with a long-term goal like buying a house.

Where we lived at the time was between both sets of our parents. Does that make me neurotic, because we wanted equal access to our parents? No. Living there had other benefits too, but that was something we wanted to take into consideration.

So I don't personally see that as a polyvagal thing. Deciding to live in the middle is a decision. You did decide. That's weighing pros and cons. That's being able to notice, "I want this and I want this, and here's my solution." That's fantastic.
Not being able to decide is where there may be some polyvagal implications.

Let's get rid of the muffin examples. Say you have an impulse to upgrade your life. You want a new job, or you want to take on a new hobby, and you don't know what to do. That may be an issue of not knowing what speaks to you and your system. It may be an issue of not knowing what safety feels like.

Say you want a new hobby. You like to journal, but you also like to draw. Which one do you go toward? At that point, I think it's about listening to what you feel inside of you. What feels like it would be the most helpful? Where is your impulse going?

With the polyvagal stuff, it might be difficult to notice that feeling, that impulse toward safety. It might also be difficult to notice that surging motivation. Motivation, to me, is having flight and fight energy active along with your safety pathways. You feel energized, but it's not out-of-control mobilization. You feel it and you're able to harness it and use it. Discipline is then being able to point it in a certain direction.

So I think it's important to notice those little somatic impulses inside of us, and to notice what feels safest, especially if you're using the hobby as a means to self-regulate. But those impulses toward safety are hard to notice. What we may notice instead is that we want to do something, and we get a little burst of energy.

This is something I went through a lot over the years, before I realized what I was really pulled toward. I was doing a whole bunch of stuff. I was interested in this, I was interested in that. One of those things was drawing and sketching, and content creation for a whole bunch of other things. I felt like, "Oh, I want to do this, and I want to do this, and I want to do this."
But it was kind of frantic. It was this frantic thing I couldn't keep up with, and it would spiral and then fizzle out, and that was it.

Now, with this content creation and my therapy work, it feels more genuine. I feel calmer when it comes to this, even though I'm pretty worked up right now. I feel like there's more direction. I feel more confidence, more discipline. But I had to go through those other avenues that didn't feel genuine before I realized: this isn't it, and this isn't it, and this isn't it. But this does feel right.

For a while, I was doing the art and the therapy work at the same time. It didn't work out, and I had to pick. I wanted both of those things. Does that make me neurotic? I don't think so. Maybe it made me indecisive, and maybe part of that was having motivation surge up within me back then, not being able to do anything with it, and getting pulled in different directions.

I feel differently now. I still feel that motivation, but now I have more discipline and more direction. I feel my impulse going a certain way, and I've simply been listening to it, noticing that impulse versus the other impulses that want to take me in other directions.

ul: Can we have two things at once that conflict with each other? Yes, especially on a feeling level, and it might be a good idea.
Can we want two things at the same time? Sure. That happens all the time.
Can we pick one or the other? Yes, though we might have to sacrifice one.
Can we pick an option in the middle of both? Absolutely.
